display.story_text:
Kent State vs Eastern Michigan closes both seasons on a Tuesday night in Ypsilanti, and Eastern Michigan is pricing it to fill seats: seven-dollar tickets, concession specials and a Senior Night that honors thirty members of the program on Crosby Field. My Kent State vs Eastern Michigan pick is Eastern Michigan Eagles −6.5 with the Over 46.5, even though the best-known senior on that list probably won't take a snap.

That senior is Noah Kim. He hasn't played since the Oct. 17 loss to Toledo, and Ypsilanti 11 reports coach Chris Creighton said this week he doesn't think it's likely Kim plays. Brogan McCaughey has taken the most throws in all three games since, and he went 12 for 16 for 135 yards in the 34-27 loss at Western Michigan. I'm pricing McCaughey, and I'm fine with it, because Eastern's offense now runs through the backfield.

Imogen Tremblay agrees, mostly. "Seven dollars a seat. For that money you get a Senior Night, a running back who doesn't go down on first contact, and me yelling about both."

Ozzie Brannigan has made the drive up from Kent and is already braced for impact. "We scored three points at home last week. Three. I've been emotionally prepared for anything since September."

Amareon Blue is the case for the side. He carried 27 times for 160 yards and 3 touchdowns in Kalamazoo, and he has 607 yards on the season. Kent State gives up 4.2 yards a carry and 29.8 points a game, and its own ground game manages 2.9 a carry. When the Flashes can't run, Dru DeShields has to throw into trouble, and he has 10 interceptions to go with 11 touchdown throws. Kent State scores 14.5 a game and sits ninth in the MAC.

The total went up a point, and I'm still on the Over. As of 5:13 PM ET Tuesday, DraftKings has Eastern Michigan Eagles −6.5 and 46.5, and my 47 gets past it. Wayne Harris, with 863 receiving yards and 7 touchdowns, is how Kent gets its points. Six of Eastern's eleven games went past 46.5. Kent has scored 10 or fewer in seven of eleven, so it's close, but a one-point move on the total doesn't talk me out of it.

The room agrees on Eastern and goes two to one for the Over. The Formula has 28-19 and Next Man Up has 29-18, and both like Eastern Michigan Eagles −6.5 and go Over 46.5. Letdown Watch has 28-18, likes the same side and goes Under 46.5. In The Trenches has no pick. Follow The Money likes Eastern Michigan Eagles −6.5 and has no total pick.

Next Man Up: "Twenty-nine for Eastern. Letdown Watch knocked a point off because somebody got misty about the seniors."

Letdown Watch: "I knocked it off because Kent State still has Wayne Harris, Next Man Up. Read past the depth chart once in a while."

My final is Eastern Michigan Eagles 29, Kent State Golden Flashes 18. Eleven points clears the 6.5 with room to spare, and 47 combined gets past the 46.5 by half a point. Blue gets the carries, the seniors get their walk, and Ozzie gets a quiet ride back to Ohio.

Eastern Michigan Eagles 29, Kent State Golden Flashes 18. Eastern Michigan Eagles cover the 6.5. Over 46.5.

display.fanatic_story:
Kent State Golden Flashes vs Eastern Michigan Eagles is a Tuesday-night goodbye in Ypsilanti, where Eastern Michigan is calling it 734 Night: seven-dollar seats inside "The Factory" at Rynearson Stadium and 30 members of the program walking onto Crosby Field for Senior Night before the 7 p.m. kickoff. Imogen Tremblay plans to clap for every single name, then spend four quarters making sure Ozzie Brannigan drives home to Kent with nothing but a ticket stub and a long face.

Neither of these teams is headed to a bowl game, and nobody in either section is pretending otherwise. This one is about the last walk off the field, and which group of seniors gets to make it smiling.

"Seven bucks," Imogen says, waving her ticket like it's a winning raffle stub. "Seven bucks to watch the Eagles beat Kent State for the fourth straight time. They should charge twenty. I'd still come."

"Fourth? You've won three," Ozzie says.

"I'm counting Tuesday early. I'm efficient."

She has a point about the recent history, and Ozzie knows it. Eastern beat Kent State 31-24 in 2022, 28-14 in 2023 and 52-33 in 2024. Kent State still holds the overall series, 19-17, per Eastern's own game notes, and Ozzie brings that up the way some people bring up a grandfather who fought in a war.

"Nineteen to seventeen," he says. "Look it up. It's in your own handout."

There is a quiet part of the night, too, and Imogen doesn't joke about it. Noah Kim is on that senior list. He hasn't played since the Toledo game in October, and coach Chris Creighton told reporters this week he doesn't think it's likely Kim plays Tuesday. Kim has been a captain, a leader and a big reason Eastern started 3-0 in the MAC.

"Whatever he's wearing, pads or a parka, he gets the loudest noise of the night," Imogen says. "Then Brogan McCaughey goes out and plays like he's been here five years."

McCaughey has taken over, and he was sharp in Kalamazoo last week, 12 of 16 for 135 yards. But the guy Imogen really wants to talk about is Amareon Blue. Blue carried 27 times for 160 yards and three touchdowns against Western Michigan, and he looked like a guy who had decided he wasn't going down without company.

"He runs angry," Imogen says. "Angry and short. They can't find him behind the big guys until he's already past them."

Ozzie's answer is Wayne Harris. Harris has 863 receiving yards and seven touchdowns, and when Dru DeShields has time, Harris is the first place the ball goes. DeShields threw for 332 yards at Bowling Green and four touchdowns in the 35-20 win over Akron, a game Ozzie has watched more times than he will admit to his family.

"When Dru and Wayne get going, we're a different team," Ozzie says. "The trick is getting them going before halftime. We've been working on that trick since Labor Day."

The trouble is up front. Kent State has had a hard time moving the ball on the ground all year, and when the Flashes can't run, DeShields ends up throwing into crowds. Last week on their own Senior Night, Kent managed three points against Miami.

"Don't remind me," Ozzie says. "My seniors deserved better. My seniors deserve your seniors losing on their night, just to even it out."

"That's not how fairness works, Ozzie."

"It's how it works in Kent."

Eastern's defense has a couple of names Ozzie keeps an eye on. Quincy Byas leads the Eagles with five sacks, and Bryce Llewellyn, another senior being honored, leads the team in tackles. Linebacker Zach Mowchan, a captain, has 67 tackles of his own. On the other side, Jaihien Roy has six sacks for Kent State, and Hayden Dawahare leads the Flashes in stops.

Here's how Tuesday goes. Eastern hands the ball to Blue early and often, and the cheap seats get loud in a hurry. Kent State hangs around in the first half because Harris gets loose down the sideline once and DeShields finds him for a touchdown. But Byas gets home twice in the second half, the Eagles grind out the clock with Blue, and Llewellyn makes one last big tackle in front of the home crowd to end Kent's last real chance. The Flashes add a late score to give Ozzie something for the drive back.

When it's over, the seniors make one more lap toward the student section, and Imogen holds her seven-dollar stub up next to her face for a picture, the cheapest souvenir she's ever kept and the one she'll never throw out.

My call: Eastern Michigan Eagles 29, Kent State Golden Flashes 18.

Western Michigan is handing out free tickets to Tuesday night's regular-season finale at Waldo Stadium, courtesy of Greenleaf Trust, Greenleaf Hospitality and Ziegler Auto Group, because the Broncos want Kalamazoo packed for a rematch of last December's MAC title game. My Miami (OH) vs Western Michigan pick is Western Michigan Broncos −4.5 and the Over 45.5: a full house, a hungry ground game, and a RedHawks offense on its third quarterback of the year.

Corwin Dahlquist has been forwarding the ticket link to everyone in his phone. "Free seat, Jalen Buckley, and the team that beat you in Detroit. Best deal in Kalamazoo this week, and nobody else is close."

Cordelia Van Doren is not impressed by the giveaway. "Generous of you, Corwin. We'll take the seats, the win, and the trip back to Detroit."

Detroit is the sore spot. Western Michigan beat Miami 23-13 in that title game last December, and Miami can only get back there with a win on Tuesday plus some tiebreaker help elsewhere. Chasing a game is hard without a settled quarterback. David McComb has the most passing yards on the team at 1,121, Caleb Heavner took the snaps through the middle of the year, and true freshman Drew Bellisari has run the offense the last two weeks. Bellisari went 7 of 12 for 124 yards in the 20-3 win at Kent State, and Miami rode D'Shawntae Jones for 29 carries and 121 yards that night. That's a team protecting a young quarterback, not turning him loose.

Western Michigan doesn't have that problem. Broc Lowry has 1,652 yards, 12 touchdowns and 3 interceptions. Jalen Buckley has 972 yards and 12 touchdowns, including 140 yards and two scores against Eastern Michigan last week. The Broncos are 8-3, 6-1 in the league, scoring 28.4 points a game and allowing 19.5. They have won every league game at Waldo this year.

My margin of nine comes from that quarterback gap. Miami's defense will make Buckley earn the first half, but a freshman on the road who needs points late is how a one-score game turns into two.

The Over is the closer call. I have 47, a point and a half past the number. Miami's games have gone over 45.5 in 7 of 11, and Western Michigan put up 34 on Eastern Michigan last week. DraftKings opened Western Michigan −7.5 with a 46.5 total, and as of 5:13 PM ET Tuesday it sits at −4.5 and 45.5.

The room is split. The Formula has Western Michigan 28-22, takes Western Michigan Broncos −4.5 and likes the Over 45.5. Next Man Up has 28-17, likes Western Michigan Broncos −4.5 and goes Under. Letdown Watch has 29-18, likes the Broncos and goes Over. In The Trenches has no score this week, sees the fronts as split, and takes neither side nor total. Follow The Money likes Miami (OH) RedHawks +4.5 and has no total pick.

Next Man Up: "The Formula finally came around on the Broncos. Took that spreadsheet long enough."

The Formula: "Six points of daylight, Next Man Up. You'll be sweating that Under by halftime."

My final is Western Michigan Broncos 28, Miami (OH) RedHawks 19. Cordelia checks her tiebreaker math on the bus anyway.

display.fanatic_story:
Nobody in Kalamazoo has an excuse to skip Tuesday night, because Western Michigan is giving away tickets to the last home game of the year at Waldo Stadium. Miami (OH) RedHawks vs Western Michigan Broncos is a rematch of last December's MAC title game, and Corwin Dahlquist has spent the week texting the free-ticket link to guys he hasn't talked to since high school while Cordelia Van Doren packs a red scarf and a grudge in Oxford.

"Free," Corwin says. "Greenleaf Trust, Greenleaf Hospitality, Ziegler Auto Group. I want to shake every one of their hands. I want Waldo so loud your freshman hears it through his helmet."

"Pack it," Cordelia says. "We like an audience."

Here's what the free seats get you. Jalen Buckley, a redshirt senior who just moved into third in program history with 40 rushing touchdowns, took the first snap against Eastern Michigan last week and went 72 yards to the end zone. It was the third game in a row a Bronco back broke a run of at least 72 yards, after Cole Cabana went 82 against Akron and again against Bowling Green. Buckley finished with 140 yards and two scores, and Western Michigan beat Eastern 34-27 to keep the Michigan MAC Trophy for a fourth straight season.

"Fourth straight," Corwin says. "Central, Eastern, sit down. That's a full stack, and I'm pouring the syrup."

"You won a trophy for beating two schools from your own state," Cordelia says. "Congratulations. We own the series. Thirty-nine wins to your twenty-five, with a tie in there to keep it polite."

She's right about the history, and Corwin knows it. He also knows what happened the last time these two met: Western Michigan 23, Miami 13, in Detroit, with a championship on the table. That's the one Cordelia doesn't bring up at Thanksgiving.

Miami shows up with plenty at stake. The RedHawks are 7-4 and 5-2 in the league, and they need a win in Kalamazoo plus some tiebreaker help elsewhere to get back to Detroit for a fourth trip in a row. They're doing it on their third quarterback of the season. Drew Bellisari is a true freshman who stepped in against Ohio and then ran the show at Kent State, a 20-3 win where Miami handed the ball to D'Shawntae Jones 29 times for 121 yards and two touchdowns.

"Miami is the Cradle of Coaches," Cordelia says. "We have been teaching young men how to win in November since before your school had a paper engineering program. Our freshman will be fine."

Here's the part that keeps Corwin up at night. Miami's defense stops the run better than anybody in the MAC, giving up 94.8 yards a game, 13th in the country. Malcolm McCain has 90 tackles. Grant Lyons has 7 sacks. Amariyun Knighten has three interceptions and 14 breakups, second in the nation in passes defended. And then there's Scoop Smith, a freshman receiver who has already taken a punt and a kickoff back for touchdowns.

"Scoop Smith scares me," Corwin admits. "I want every kick out of bounds. I don't care if it costs us twenty yards."

His answer is the linebackers. Western Michigan's linebackers have five of the team's eight interceptions, and senior Dillon Moore has three of them, including one he ran back for a touchdown against Eastern Michigan. Justyce Betts leads the team with 69 tackles, and Scoop Gardner Jr. has 6 sacks coming off the end. A freshman quarterback who has to throw in the fourth quarter is exactly what that group has been waiting for all month.

Broc Lowry doesn't have to be a hero, either. He has 1,652 yards with 12 touchdown throws and 3 interceptions, and he went 15 for 15 at Akron two weeks ago. Lance Taylor is already the second coach in Western Michigan history with eight wins in back-to-back seasons, next to PJ Fleck. One more and he stands alone.

"Row the boat," Corwin says. "Then row it again."

"Fleck," Cordelia says, and smiles. "Another coach who left. You do produce them."

Here's how Tuesday goes. Miami's front keeps Buckley quiet for a half, Jones grinds the clock, and it's a one-score game at the break with Cordelia doing tiebreaker math on a napkin. Then the Broncos wear the RedHawks down. Lowry finds Aveion Chenault on third down, Buckley breaks a long one in the third quarter, and Moore's group gets its shot at a freshman who has to throw. Miami scores late to make the bus ride quieter, not to change anything.

Corwin walks out holding a ticket stub that cost him nothing, and he's putting it in a frame anyway.

My call: Western Michigan Broncos 28, Miami (OH) RedHawks 19.

display.fanatic_story:
Debbie McGuire will stand on the Galaxy Stadium grass Thursday night next to her husband and a long row of Red Raider families, and Bodie Ratliff plans to be in his seat early enough to clap for every senior by name. Ryder Galloway drove up from Fort Worth for TCU Horned Frogs vs Texas Tech Red Raiders with a team that changed head coaches on Sunday, and he says he'll clap for the seniors too, right up until the opening kickoff.

"Thanksgiving night in Lubbock," Bodie says. "Senior Day. Ten wins already. My mama's bringing two pies and a folding chair she does not need, because nobody sits down in this building."

"Nobody sits down because the wind would take the chair," Ryder says.

Bodie lets that one go. Anybody raised on the South Plains has chased a hat or two across a parking lot.

The Red Raiders have earned the swagger. Texas Tech is 10-1, unbeaten at home, and the only loss came at Cincinnati back in October. Since Thomas Castellanos took over the throwing, the offense has turned every Saturday into a track meet. He threw for 362 yards and five touchdowns in the 53-48 shootout with West Virginia, then 263 yards and four more at Oklahoma State. Behind him, J'Koby Williams has run for 1,195 yards and 9 touchdowns, and he went for 117 in the 20-10 win at Baylor last week.

"You see what Castellanos does on a third down?" Bodie asks. "He looks at the defense like it owes him money."

Ryder knows what Castellanos does. He watched it on a small screen in a Fort Worth kitchen and didn't enjoy one minute of it.

The week in Fort Worth has been something else. TCU fired Sonny Dykes on Sunday, four years after he took the Frogs to the national title game, and handed the team to defensive coordinator Andy Avalos for the finale. The Frogs are 5-6. One more win means a bowl trip. One more loss means the offseason starts Friday morning.

"So here's the part you're missing," Ryder says. "Avalos runs the defense. The defense is the reason we're still standing. We've given up 17.3 a game. We lost to North Carolina by five, UCF by eight, BYU by seven, West Virginia by four and Arizona by one. Every one of those came down to a drive."

"And Utah?"

"We don't talk about Utah."

That was a 38-17 loss at home Saturday, and it's the one game all season the TCU defense didn't hang around. The other question is who's throwing. Jaden Craig handled the job for most of the year and has 2,664 yards and 13 touchdowns, with Kari Ashley as his go-to tight end at 697 yards. Against Utah, Adam Schobel took the throws. Ryder figures whoever takes the snaps needs to hand it to Jeremy Payne, who ran for 108 yards and two scores even in the blowout, and get out of the way.

"Keep it on the ground," Ryder says. "Shorten the game. Make Castellanos sit on the bench and think about it."

On defense, the Frogs need Koron Hayward, who has 7 sacks, and Hudson Hooper, who leads the team with 79 tackles, to make Williams work for every yard. Bodie's counter is A.J. Holmes Jr., who has 10 sacks and has spent the fall living in other people's backfields, and Austin Romaine, who has 95 tackles and seems to show up on every snap.

"Ryder, I like you," Bodie says. "I want you to know that before the third quarter."

Here's how I see the night. TCU's defense comes out angry and plays for its interim coach like it means it, and the first half is closer than anybody in the south end zone wants. Payne breaks a long run, the Frogs kick a field goal, and the TCU section gets loud enough to hear from the press box. But Castellanos finds Kenny Johnson down the sideline before halftime, Williams starts leaning on a tired front in the third, and Holmes gets home on a third down that flips the field.

The Frogs make it a game into the fourth quarter. They just can't make it a win. The seniors walk off unbeaten at home, and Ryder drives back down to Fort Worth, waiting to hear who's coaching his team next.

Bodie walks him to the parking lot anyway, still holding one of his mama's pies, and hands it over without a word.

My call: Texas Tech Red Raiders 30, TCU Horned Frogs 18.

display.fanatic_story:
Mississippi State Bulldogs vs Ole Miss Rebels is the 123rd Egg Bowl, and for the second straight year it kicks off at 11 a.m. on Black Friday, early enough that half of Starkville will be on the road to Oxford before the sun clears the pines. Wade Pettus is in that caravan with his cowbell wrapped in a dish towel so it won't wake the neighbors, and he's driving west to look Langston Fairbanks in the eye after three straight years of hearing about it.

Langston has been counting those years out loud since Sunday.

"Three," he says, holding up fingers like a man ordering at a drive-thru. "Three Egg Bowls in a row. You know the last time we did that? Two thousand two through two thousand four. I was in grade school. It felt great then, too."

"And you know the last time you won four straight?" Wade says. "When the game was still played in Jackson. You're asking history for a big favor, Langston."

"History owes me one," Langston says. "I sat through some long Novembers."

Wade lets him have the joke, because Wade is in a generous mood for the first time in a month and a half. The Bulldogs had dropped six in a row before last Saturday, when they beat Tennessee Tech 34-16 at Davis Wade Stadium. Parker Puckett threw for 232 yards and two touchdowns, Anthony Evans III caught eight balls for 129 yards, and Xavier Gayten broke off 100 yards on three carries, which Wade has watched so many times his phone thinks it's a ringtone.

"Three carries, a hundred yards," Wade says. "That's thirty-three yards a pop. I did the math in the parking lot."

"You did math with a cowbell in your hand?"

"I can do anything with a cowbell in my hand."

Langston's answer is a quarterback. Trinidad Chambliss went 19 for 20 against Wofford last Saturday for 367 yards and five touchdowns, and Deuce Alexander caught two of them on a 128-yard afternoon. Chambliss has 2,853 yards and 24 touchdown throws this year, and in the Grove they talk about him the way Oxford talks about its writers, like he belongs on a plaque somewhere off the Square.

"Nineteen of twenty," Langston says. "The one he missed, the receiver sent a handwritten apology."

"Georgia beat you 42-7," Wade says. "Oklahoma held him to 127 yards in Norman. Your guy is a great story when the other team rides a bus up from Spartanburg."

That one lands. Ole Miss is 7-4, and the four losses include a long afternoon in Gainesville and that Georgia game, which nobody in Oxford brings up unless they're asked twice. The Rebels get their pressure from Blake Purchase, who has six sacks, and Tah'j Butler is all over the field from linebacker with 65 tackles. Kewan Lacy is the leading rusher, and he's listed out for Friday, so the backs behind him get their turn. When this team is rolling, the Grove gets loud before noon, which on Friday is the only time there will be.

Mississippi State has been through three quarterbacks. Kamario Taylor was on fire early, with 17 touchdown throws and only four interceptions in the first five games, and Wade still has the Minnesota win saved on his phone. Then came Puckett, then AJ Swann, then Puckett again. Through all of it, Evans kept catching the ball. He has 73 grabs for 929 yards, and Fluff Bothwell has run for 649. On defense, Jardin Gilbert leads the team with 70 tackles and Jaray Bledsoe has 5.5 sacks.

"The Bulldogs are going to play loose," Wade says. "Nobody gave us a chance in October. Nobody's giving us one now. That's the best kind of Friday."

"The best kind of Friday is a three-game run turning into four," Langston says. "Bring your bell. It'll sound sad in our stadium. Real sad. Like a dinner bell nobody answers."

Here's how it goes. Chambliss opens like he's still playing Wofford and hits Alexander deep, and Ole Miss goes up two scores before the first quarter ends. Puckett answers with Evans on a long catch-and-run, and the cowbells start rattling in the visiting section like a hardware store in a hailstorm. The Bulldogs hang around into the third quarter, close enough that Wade starts texting his brother-in-law, but Purchase gets home twice in the second half, the Rebels grind out a long drive, and the Rebels pull away. Mississippi State gets a late touchdown that matters to every Bulldog who made the drive, and Gilbert makes enough tackles that Wade leaves proud anyway.

Langston will hold up four fingers on the walk to the car, practicing for next year. Wade will ring the bell once, loud, right behind his ear.

My call: Ole Miss Rebels 35, Mississippi State Bulldogs 21.

Nebraska Cornhuskers vs Iowa Hawkeyes on Black Friday is the Pioneer Heroes Game, and before kickoff at Kinnick Stadium one everyday hero from Iowa and one from Nebraska will be honored on the field and have their names inscribed on the Heroes Trophy. Darla Rasmussen drove in from Lincoln still floating from the Ohio State win, and Orrin Kalvelage met her in the parking lot at sunrise to remind her that floating and winning in Iowa City are two different things.

"Six in the morning," Orrin says. "That's when the lots open. I was here at five-fifty. That's how you respect Senior Day."

"I didn't sleep," Darla says. "I'm not tired. I don't think I'll ever be tired again. We beat Ohio State, Orrin. Thirty-one to twenty-eight. Anthony Colandrea threw three touchdowns. Do you know what that feels like?"

"I know what it feels like to hold that trophy," Orrin says, and he points at the stadium like it's a family farm.

That's where the needling starts, because the recent history between these two programs is not much of a fight. Iowa has won nine of the last ten meetings. Last year it was 40-16. The two years before that were 13-10 and 13-10, which is about as Iowa as football gets.

"Thirteen to ten twice in a row," Darla says. "That's not a rivalry. That's a hostage situation."

"It's a love language," Orrin says.

What makes this one different is that Darla's team arrives with real momentum. Nebraska went through a hard stretch in October, four straight losses, three of them by a touchdown or less, and it looked like the season was getting away. Then the Huskers went to Rutgers and won 31-0, came home and knocked off Ohio State, and suddenly Colandrea looks like the guy Darla promised everyone in August. He has 21 touchdown throws and only seven interceptions. Kwazi Gilmer has eight touchdown catches, and Jamal Rule has 705 rushing yards.

"We figured something out," Darla says. "And you know what we figured out? We can score on anybody."

"You can score on Rutgers," Orrin says. "Come score on us."

He has reason to talk. Iowa's defense has given up 12.2 points a game this season. It shut out Northern Illinois, Northern Iowa and Wisconsin. Linebacker Cam Buffington has 97 tackles, and Orrin can tell you where every one of them happened. The Hawkeyes have lost twice, to Ohio State and by three points at Minnesota, and they are No. 15 in the country coming into the last home game of the year.

Then there's the part of Kinnick that gets Darla every time, even when she's rooting against it. The Swarm, with the players arm in arm and coming out together, the way Hayden Fry started it. The I-O-W-A chant moving corner to corner after every score. And somewhere in the middle of it, a fan trying to win the Pancheros Burrito Lift on the big screen by hoisting his buddy over his head.

"I'm not doing the burrito," Darla says.

"Nobody asked you to be the burrito," Orrin says. "You'd have to earn that."

Iowa's offense is never going to make a highlight show, and Orrin is fine with that. Hank Brown runs it carefully, with 10 touchdown throws and four interceptions, and the Hawkeyes trust the ground game when it matters. Last week L.J. Phillips Jr. ran for 154 yards at Illinois in a 34-17 win.

"We run the ball, we punt it deep, we hit you," Orrin says. "If you want fireworks, there's a Fourth of July."

The Nebraska worry is the week itself. The Huskers poured everything into last Saturday, and now they have to turn around and play a Friday road game in a stadium that will be loud from the Hawk Walk on. Darla knows it. She just won't say it.

Here's how Friday goes. Nebraska comes out loose and confident, and Colandrea finds Gilmer for an early touchdown that quiets the student section for about four seconds. Iowa answers on the ground, Phillips grinds out a long drive, and the I-O-W-A chant goes around twice before halftime. In the second half the Hawkeyes' defense does what it does, squeezing the field until Colandrea is throwing into coverage on third down. Nebraska keeps it close until late, then Iowa runs out the last five minutes with the ball on the ground.

Darla gets one good look at the Heroes Trophy as it goes past her, close enough to read both names on it, and she tells Orrin the honest truth: the real heroes on it were the only part of the day she didn't argue with.

My call: Iowa Hawkeyes 24, Nebraska Cornhuskers 18.

Tulsa has never played a football game in San Antonio, and its first trip lands on UTSA's Senior Day, an 11 a.m. local kickoff at the Alamodome on Black Friday. My Tulsa vs UTSA pick is UTSA Roadrunners +1.5 and the Under 57.5, because the Roadrunners haven't lost in that building this year and the last month of their football has been a grind, not a track meet.

Marisol Ybarra has her day planned. "Seniors at eleven, River Parade at six. I'll be on the River Walk with a medal around my neck for every senior who walks out of that tunnel."

Wiley Pettibone came down from Tulsa ready to talk about 2024. "Forty-six to forty-five, Marisol. We came back on you. Baylor Hayes is throwing better than anybody you've seen this month."

He isn't wrong about Hayes. The Tulsa quarterback has 2,275 yards with 20 touchdowns and 4 interceptions, and he threw four scores against Charlotte last week in a 42-14 win. Oran Singleton Jr. has 70 catches, 891 yards and 10 touchdowns, three of them on Saturday. Tulsa is 7-4, scoring 34.4 points a game, and it has won three straight by a combined 140-45.

So why the Roadrunners? Because the building matters and so does the shape of their season. UTSA is 9-2, 6-1 in the American, and unbeaten at the Alamodome. The Roadrunners have also won their last two by grinding: 35-16 over North Texas and 19-17 at UAB, with Owen McCown throwing for 85 yards in one and 112 in the other. Will Henderson III carried 23 times at UAB. That's a team that wants to shorten the game. The line has flipped, so UTSA is now getting a point and a half at home, and a team that wins close games in its own building is the one I'll take with points.

That's also the Under case. McCown has 2,213 yards and 13 touchdowns, and he can throw it around when he has to, but UTSA has chosen not to lately. Tulsa's defense has allowed 10, 21 and 14 points in its last three games, and Kyran Duhon has 8 sacks for a front that will make McCown hold the ball. I have 56, a point and a half under the number.

DraftKings opened UTSA Roadrunners −2.5 and 58.5. As of 6:11 AM ET Friday it's Tulsa Golden Hurricane −1.5 and 57.5.

Follow The Money takes Tulsa Golden Hurricane −1.5 and the Under 57.5.

The Formula: "My number didn't move. The line did. I still have a one-point game, and now the hook is on my side."

My final is UTSA Roadrunners 29, Tulsa Golden Hurricane 27. Marisol makes the six o'clock parade. Wiley drives home composing a long text about 2024.

display.fanatic_story:
San Antonio is going to be busy on Black Friday, with UTSA's Senior Day at 11 in the morning and the 45th Ford Holiday River Parade floating down the River Walk at 6 that night. Tulsa Golden Hurricane vs UTSA Roadrunners squeezes into the middle of all that, and it's the first time Tulsa football has ever come to San Antonio, which Marisol Ybarra treats as a personal invitation and Wiley Pettibone treats as a road trip with unfinished business.

"Welcome to the Alamodome," Marisol says. "Park early. Downtown is going to be wall to wall by lunch, and the seniors get one more walk out of that tunnel before you even find your seats."

"I'll find mine," Wiley says. "I've been waiting two years to sit in them."

Two years ago in Tulsa, the Golden Hurricane rallied and beat UTSA 46-45, and Wiley still describes that afternoon like a man who struck oil in his own backyard. UTSA won the first meeting back in 2013, 34-15, but nobody in Oklahoma is bringing that one up this week.

Here's why Wiley drove down I-35 smiling. Baylor Hayes is playing the best football of anybody in this game. He threw four touchdowns against Charlotte last Saturday, and Oran Singleton Jr. caught three of them for 116 yards. Singleton has 70 catches and 10 touchdowns on the year, and he's the guy Marisol keeps circling on her program. Tulsa has won three in a row, including a 60-10 demolition at Tulane, and Trequan Jones ran for 109 yards on ten carries last week just to make sure the Charlotte defense knew it had to worry about the ground, too.

"That's three gushers in a row," Wiley says. "Hayes finds oil every time he drops back."

"Then he can drop back in front of a dome full of people who want him to stop," Marisol says.

Marisol's case is the building. UTSA hasn't lost at the Alamodome all year, and under Jeff Traylor, now in his seventh season, the Roadrunners are 38-5 at home and 28-1 against league opponents there. They sit first in the American at 6-1 with a chance to finish the job in front of their own people. That kind of home record makes visiting teams nervous before they've even unloaded the bus.

The way UTSA has been winning lately won't win any beauty contests. The Roadrunners beat North Texas 35-16 and then ground out a 19-17 win at UAB last week, with Will Henderson III carrying 23 times for 93 yards. Owen McCown has thrown for more than two thousand yards this year, but the last two weeks he's handed off, managed the game and let the defense do the heavy lifting. Darion White leads that defense with 75 tackles. Owen Pewee has 4 sacks. They don't make highlight reels every week. They make the other team's quarterback uncomfortable.

"Ugly wins count the same," Marisol says. "I've got a medal for every one of them."

"You've got a drawer full of medals," Wiley says.

"And room for more."

Wiley's worry is Tulsa's own history in close ones this year. The Golden Hurricane lost to North Texas in overtime, 45-44, and dropped a 38-35 game to Army, and both times the offense had the ball with a chance late. Hayes can throw it with anybody, but Tulsa's defense needs to stand up when McCown has to make a play on third down, and Kyran Duhon, with 8 sacks, is the guy who has to make that happen.

Here's how the morning goes. The seniors get their moment, the dome gets loud, and Tulsa answers with a quick touchdown to Singleton that quiets it for a few minutes. Henderson grinds, McCown hits one deep shot to remind everybody he can, and the game turns into a back-and-forth that has nobody leaving early for the River Walk. Tulsa gets the ball late with a chance. UTSA's front gets home on third down, and the Roadrunners run out the clock.

Marisol heads downtown to stake out a spot on the River Walk with confetti in her pocket. Wiley heads to his truck, checks the clock, and figures he can be north of Austin before the first float hits the water.

My call: UTSA Roadrunners 29, Tulsa Golden Hurricane 27.

The Zips honor their seniors at noon on Black Friday, and Buffalo rolls into Akron needing a win to keep its ticket to Detroit in play. My Buffalo vs Akron prediction for InfoCision Stadium is Buffalo Bulls −7.5 and the Over 48.5, and the Bulls have a six-game winning run behind them.

Kendra Woolcott has done the math on a napkin. "Win Friday and we're still alive for Ford Field. Lose and we're done. Hollister, I need your seniors to have a nice ceremony and then a quiet afternoon."

Hollister "Zip" Grubbs is unbothered. "We beat you last year, Kendra. Twenty-four to sixteen. And we just won at UMass. That's a winning run too. It's one game long, but it counts."

The Bulls are 8-3 and 6-1 in the MAC, and they win by running the ball until the other team quits. Messiah Burch has 1,310 rushing yards and 9 touchdowns, and he went for 200 against Central Michigan last week in a 40-21 win. Jason Wright only threw 13 times in that game. He didn't need more, but he has Chance Morrow when he does, with 710 receiving yards and 10 touchdowns.

That ground game is aimed right at Akron's soft spot. The Zips are 2-9 and allow 33.2 points a game. Western Michigan scored 42 on them in Akron two weeks ago, Central Michigan put up 41, and Miami (OH) scored 34. Akron has to stop a back like Burch from getting to the second level, and it hasn't shown that it can.

The Zips can score some. Jordan Gant has 942 rushing yards and 9 touchdowns and ran for 151 at UMass, and Cibastian Broughton has handled the throws the last three weeks. The Welcome Santa Parade rolls down South Main Street in Akron at 6 p.m. on Friday, and by then Hollister "Zip" Grubbs expects to have shaken hands with every Zips senior who walked across InfoCision Stadium at noon. Kendra Woolcott drove in from Western New York for Buffalo Bulls vs Akron Zips with one thing on her mind, and it isn't the tree lighting, the drone show or the ice bumper cars Hollister keeps telling her about.

"Detroit," she says. "Ford Field. December 5. That's my parade."

"You could do both," Hollister says. "Game at noon, parade at six. Akron on Black Friday. Nobody throws a better Friday."

"Nobody in Akron has thrown a better anything since September."

Hollister laughs, because she isn't wrong and he's from a town that knows how to take a punch. Akron is 2-9. The Zips have lost by double figures to Wake Forest, Minnesota, UNLV, Central Michigan, Miami, Kent State and Western Michigan. The defense has given up 33.2 points a game. Hollister calls the season a slow leak.

But he has one thing in his pocket, and he's going to keep pulling it out all day.

"Last week. At UMass. Thirty-four to thirty-three," he says. "And last year? We beat you. Twenty-four to sixteen. I'll remind you as often as I need to."

Kendra shakes her head. Last year doesn't play on Friday. This year does, and this year Buffalo is 8-3, 6-1 in the MAC and has won six straight. The Bulls beat Toledo in Toledo, survived Miami in overtime, and just ran over Central Michigan 40-21. Messiah Burch carried 24 times for 200 yards and two touchdowns in that one, and he has 1,310 yards on the season.

"Messiah runs like he's late for something," Kendra says. "He's not dancing. He's not looking for the camera. He's going north until somebody stops him, and most of the time nobody does."

Jason Wright has been the man throwing it all year, with 1,545 yards and 11 touchdowns, and Chance Morrow has caught 10 of them. On defense, SaVeon Brown leads the Bulls with 90 tackles and Will Clark has 3.5 sacks off the end. The plan hasn't changed since September: run it, hit Morrow when the safeties creep up, hang on in the fourth quarter.

The catch is that Buffalo can't do this alone. Western Michigan, Toledo, Buffalo and Ohio are all 6-1 in the league, and Kendra spent Sunday night going through every way it can shake out. A loss to Akron and the season's done. A win, and she needs Miami to beat Western Michigan on Tuesday or Ohio to beat Toledo at the same hour the Bulls kick off on Friday, or a couple of other scores to fall her way.

"I'm going to have three screens going," she says. "Ours, Athens and my phone."

Hollister has heard enough about Detroit. He'd rather talk about the seniors. Jordan Gant has run for 942 yards and 9 touchdowns and went for 151 at UMass. Cibastian Broughton has taken the throws for three weeks. Donelius Johnson has 101 tackles and plays like he's personally offended by every first down. Cyrus Durham has 4 sacks up front.

"These kids didn't quit," Hollister says. "Two wins, and they're still coming to work. That's an Akron thing. We don't get a lot of easy years here."

Here's how I see it. Akron's seniors get their moment before kickoff, the crowd is louder than a 2-9 crowd has any right to be, and Gant breaks a long one in the first quarter to make Kendra check her phone twice. Buffalo answers the way it always does. Burch carries on four straight snaps, Wright finds Morrow in the end zone, and by halftime the Bulls have a two-score cushion. The Zips keep swinging. Gant scores again, Broughton hits a big one over the middle, and the fourth quarter has a little life in it. Buffalo doesn't blink.

Kendra spends the last five minutes watching Athens on her phone. Hollister spends them walking her to the car, then turns around and heads downtown alone, so he can stand on South Main Street at six and watch the lights come on for the seniors who never got many easy Saturdays.

My call: Buffalo Bulls 31, Akron Zips 21.

display.fanatic_story:
Toledo Rockets vs Ohio Bobcats is Fan Appreciation Day at Peden Stadium on Black Friday, and Ohio has asked everybody in Athens to fill the place with green for the home finale. Penny Trautman has traded last week's black boots for a green flannel and green socks, and Rocco Szczepanski is rolling up Richland Avenue across the Hocking River with the Toledo flag still zip-tied to his antenna and a cooler full of Tony Packo's hot dogs that he promises are for sharing.

The lots open at 7 a.m. Rocco is idling at the gate before the attendant has his coffee.

"No charcoal grills," Penny says, reading off her phone like a hall monitor. "Says so right here. Tailgating in the grass next to your spot only."

"I'm not grilling," Rocco says. "These are already cooked. I drove them in from Toledo in an insulated bag. They traveled better than your offense does."

Penny lets that one go, because Penny knows what Friday is. These two teams are both 6-1 in the MAC. Toledo is 9-2. Ohio is 8-3. Whatever happens in Athens is going to hang over the whole conference for a week.

"You know the last time you were in this stadium?" Penny says. "Twenty twenty-four. We beat you 24-7. I still have the program."

"And you know what happened in that championship game two years before that? Seventeen to seven. Our way. I don't keep a program. I keep a grudge."

"That's not very Thanksgiving of you."

"It's Friday. Thanksgiving was yesterday."

Rocco is feeling good because his defense has stopped allowing points altogether. The Rockets beat Massachusetts 24-0 and Bowling Green 19-0, and Andrew Zock has 12.5 sacks from the end of that front, the kind of season that turns a quarterback's Saturday into a long afternoon of looking over his shoulder. Julian Fox has 89 tackles at linebacker. Toledo gives up 20 points a game, and lately it's been giving up nothing.

"Zock is coming," Rocco says. "You can wear green. You can wear orange. He's still coming."

"Michael Molnar has 106 tackles and seven sacks," Penny says. "He's not a linebacker, he's a weather system."

That's fair. Molnar is the heart of the Ohio defense, and the Bobcats have won eight games with a quarterback room that has changed hands more than once. Matt Vezza took most of the September snaps, Nick Poulos has carried most of it since October, and Riley Neer has 52 catches for 717 yards no matter who's throwing. Duncan Brune runs hard with 563 yards and six scores. Ohio scored 35 on Ball State last week, and the Bobcats beat Jacksonville State in overtime back in September, so Penny has seen this team survive a little chaos.

"We like it messy," Penny says. "We've been messy all year. Messy works."

"Messy didn't work at Miami."

Penny takes a long breath. The 34-17 loss in Oxford, Ohio, earlier this month is the one stain on the Bobcats' conference season, and she doesn't want to talk about it in a green flannel.

Toledo's offense is the reason Rocco keeps grinning. John Alan Richter has thrown for 2,692 yards with 20 touchdowns and three interceptions, and he threw for 429 yards in that wild 49-48 overtime win over Temple in September. Adjatay Dabbs has eight touchdown catches and CJ Miller has 862 rushing yards. The only teams to beat Toledo were Michigan State in the opener and Buffalo in October.

"He doesn't throw it to the other team," Rocco says. "Three interceptions all year. You could count them on one glove."

"You could count your manners on one glove too."

Here's how it plays out. The green crowd is loud from the first snap, and Ohio comes out running Brune right at the Toledo front, drawing first blood on a long drive that has Penny waving her socks over her head. Richter answers with Dabbs over the middle, and the two teams trade scores into halftime. Molnar gets to Richter once in the third quarter and the Peden crowd nearly comes over the rail. But Zock takes over late, Miller grinds out the clock, and Toledo kicks a field goal with a few minutes left to stretch the lead. Ohio scores once more, Neer making a catch that will be on every Athens phone by sundown, and it isn't enough.

Penny will unzip her green flannel in the parking lot. Rocco will hand her a Packo's dog, still warm, and tell her it's a peace offering until next year.

My call: Toledo Rockets 28, Ohio Bobcats 23.

App State Mountaineers vs South Alabama Jaguars was supposed to be a Saturday game, but it got moved to Black Friday, and now Hancock Whitney Stadium throws its Senior Day the afternoon after Thanksgiving with a 2 p.m. kickoff. Azalea Fairhope-Grice plans to hug every Jaguar senior she can reach, and Zeb Coldiron plans to sit very still in the visitors' section and let his defense do all of his talking.

Mobile is a little sleepy that Friday. The city buses aren't running for the holiday, and the Turkey Trot for Hope runners who took off from Mardi Gras Park on Thanksgiving morning have gone home to sleep off the stuffing. Azalea ran the 5K. She wants credit for it.

"I ran three miles on Thursday so I could yell for three hours on Friday," she says. "That's called training, Zeb."

"I drove down from the mountains on Thursday," Zeb says. "I'd call that training too."

The seniors are what Azalea really came for. South Alabama sat at 4-5 after a two-point loss at Louisiana in early November, and the season could have slipped away right there. Instead the Jaguars beat Troy 27-14 at home and then won a 40-35 track meet at Southern Miss. That got them to six wins, and it means this group gets to walk out on Senior Day with a bowl game still to look forward to.

"Six wins, and they did it the hard way," Azalea says. "Like everything worth having in Mobile."

Zeb lets that one go. He has his own worries. App State is 7-4 and has won two straight, but those two wins were 20-16 at Marshall and 17-16 in overtime against UL Monroe, and Zeb's blood pressure hasn't come all the way down from either one.

"We don't win big," he says. "We win at the end. It's not good for my heart, but it's good for my character."

What App State does well is defend. Caleb Sandstrom has seven sacks off the end of that front, and linebacker Colton Phares has 90 tackles and seems to be in on every one of them. Malachi Singleton has had a steady year throwing it, with 13 touchdown throws and seven interceptions, and Sam Pickett III is the receiver he looks for when things get tight. Jaquari Lewis leads the Mountaineers with 599 rushing yards and eight touchdowns on the ground.

"Our defense makes everybody play our kind of game," Zeb says. "Slow. Patient. A lot of punting. It's how we live up in the mountains."

"Your kind of game is a nap," Azalea says. "Our kind of game is a parade."

She isn't wrong about her team's style. South Alabama scores and gets scored on in bunches. The Jaguars beat Arkansas State 56-49 and UL Monroe 52-35, and they gave up 35 to Southern Miss and still won. PJ Martin is the engine. He has 767 rushing yards and nine touchdowns, and he went for 128 yards and two scores in Hattiesburg last week. Bishop Davenport threw for 267 yards in that game without an interception, and Trae Stevenson caught six balls for 128.

"PJ runs downhill," Azalea says. "And Mobile is flat, so he has to make his own hills. That's dedication."

The last time these two met, in 2024, South Alabama won 48-14. Zeb was there. He doesn't want to talk about it, and Azalea brings it up anyway, twice, once before kickoff and once at halftime.

Here's how Friday goes. App State's defense makes the first quarter ugly, the way it likes, and Singleton finds Pickett for an early score that has Zeb standing up for the first time all day. But Martin starts finding room outside in the second quarter, and the Jaguars go into halftime with the lead. The Mountaineers keep hanging around, because that's what they do, and Lewis punches one in late to make it a one-score game. South Alabama gets the ball back, hands it to Martin four straight times and kneels it out in front of the seniors.

When it's over, Azalea gets her hugs in along the railing, and she tells Zeb the Magic Christmas in Lights at Bellingrath Gardens reopens that very night, so he might as well stay and see something in Mobile that's even brighter than the Jaguars' seniors.

My call: South Alabama Jaguars 30, App State Mountaineers 25.

Florida State's whole season comes down to Friday afternoon at Doak Campbell Stadium: it's Senior Day, the Seminoles are 5-6, and only a win over No. 24 Florida makes them bowl-eligible. My Florida vs Florida State pick is Florida State Seminoles +6.5 and the Over 53.5, with the Gators winning the game but not by enough to clear the number.

Gianna Ravello has a motion on the floor. "Senior Day, a bowl on the table, and an interim coach who wants one more home win before the transition. I move that the Seminoles keep this within a field goal, and I have the votes."

Dax Marchetti answers like he's narrating a nature film. "Observe the Gator in late November. Patient. Rested. Winner of its last two. It does not care about your motion."

Interim coach Rick Stockstill has a coaching transition coming after the season, and he said Monday that Ashton Daniels stays his quarterback. Daniels is the reason this game stays close and the reason it scores. He has 2,515 yards and 14 touchdowns, and he also has 14 interceptions, including two in last week's 28-10 loss to NC State. Micahi Danzy, with 584 receiving yards, is the deep threat. Stockstill also said he isn't confident his injured running backs will be back Friday, which pushes even more of this onto Daniels' arm.

Florida is 7-4 and back on track with Aaron Philo under center. The Gators beat Kentucky 21-14 and Vanderbilt 34-27, and Philo went 20 of 26 for 241 yards against the Commodores. Jadan Baugh has 980 yards and 16 rushing touchdowns, and he's the best player on the field. Last year in Gainesville, the Gators won 40-21.

So why take the points? A desperate home team on Senior Day with a bowl trip on the line doesn't fold in the second half. Florida's last two wins were one-score games, and six and a half points on the road in a rivalry is a lot to ask. My margin is three, which keeps Florida State inside the number even if the Gators make the last big play.

The Over comes from the turnover math. Daniels throws it to both teams, and Baugh turns short fields into touchdowns. Florida has gone over 53.5 in 7 of 11 games, and Florida State's defense is giving up 26.6 points a game. I have 55. DraftKings opened Florida −4.5 with a 52.5 total, and as of 6:13 AM ET Friday the Gators are up to −6.5 with the total at 53.5.

My final is Florida Gators 29, Florida State Seminoles 26. Dax gets his chomp. Gianna files a complaint with the replay booth.

display.fanatic_story:
Florida State's seniors walk out at Doak Campbell Stadium on Friday afternoon knowing that if they lose to the Gators, their season ends right there with no bowl game. Florida Gators vs Florida State Seminoles is Senior Day in Tallahassee, the Seminoles are sitting at five wins, and Gianna Ravello has been saying "six" out loud all week like she's trying to make it happen by repetition, while Dax Marchetti rolls up from Gainesville sounding like a man who'd love to spoil a party.

"Six," Gianna says. "Six wins, a bowl, and our first winning season in three years. Write it down. Frame it. Hang it in the Capitol."

"I've seen this before," Dax says. "The garnet-and-gold creature, cornered in its own den, makes a lot of noise. Then the Gator eats."

There's more going on in Tallahassee than a bowl chase. Rick Stockstill is the interim coach, there's a coaching transition coming after the season, and Friday is a chance for him and the staff to go out with a rivalry win in front of the home crowd. Stockstill spent his first press conference of the week telling the younger players exactly how much this game means to the people in this town, in case anybody on the roster hadn't figured it out yet.

There's a twist, too. Florida's offensive coordinator, Buster Faulkner, used to work for Stockstill at Middle Tennessee, and Stockstill called him a brilliant offensive mind on Monday. So the old boss is trying to stop the guy he helped bring up.

"That's a family reunion," Dax says. "Somebody's leaving the table hungry."

"Coach knows every trick in that playbook because he taught half of them," Gianna says. "Read the fine print, Dax."

The Gators come in hot. They've won two straight, 21-14 at Kentucky and 34-27 over Vanderbilt, and Aaron Philo looked sharp against the Commodores, going 20 of 26 for 241 yards. Jadan Baugh is the problem for any defense in the state. He has 980 yards and 16 rushing touchdowns, and he runs like he's personally offended by arm tackles. Eric Singleton Jr. caught six balls for 117 yards against Vanderbilt, and Myles Graham leads the defense with 86 tackles. Jayden Woods has 7 sacks.

"Baugh is an alligator snapping turtle," Dax says. "Slow to get going, then he takes your whole arm."

Florida State has to answer with Ashton Daniels, and Stockstill made it clear on Monday that Daniels is his guy. Daniels has 2,515 yards and 14 touchdown throws, and he's had big days: 377 yards at Alabama, 350 against Clemson, four touchdowns at Miami. He's also thrown 14 interceptions, and last week's 28-10 loss to NC State had two of them. Micahi Danzy, with 584 yards, is the guy he'll look for when it matters. Chris Jones has 85 tackles at linebacker, and Rylan Kennedy has 6 sacks up front.

"When Ashton is right, nobody in this state throws it prettier," Gianna says.

"When he's wrong, my secondary says thank you," Dax says.

The running game is where Gianna gets quiet. Stockstill said Monday it's too early to tell on his injured running backs and that he doesn't feel good about them being back for Friday. That puts a lot on Daniels and a lot on a group of senior linemen who'd love to go out pushing people around.

Last year in Gainesville, Florida won 40-21, and Dax brings it up roughly every six minutes. Gianna counters with 2022, a 45-38 Seminoles win in a shootout, and 2023, when they won again. Either way, this one has been swinging back and forth for years, and nobody on either side expects a quiet afternoon.

Here's how it goes. Doak is loud from the opening kick, Daniels hits Danzy deep in the first quarter, and the seniors play like they've been told this is their last home game, because it is. Baugh answers. Then he answers again. It's a back-and-forth game where every Seminole mistake turns into Florida points and every Florida State big play gets the place shaking. Florida gets the last real drive, Baugh grinds out the clock, and Florida State's season ends three points short with the seniors still swinging on the final snap.

Gianna sits in her seat long after the band stops, already drafting a speech about next year. Dax does a full chomp in the parking lot, then remembers where he is and does a smaller one.

My call: Florida Gators 29, Florida State Seminoles 26.

Charles Huff sends out his first Memphis senior class on Black Friday afternoon at the remodeled Simmons Bank Liberty Stadium, and the Tigers are coming off a 38-34 loss at Navy that still stings on Tiger Lane. My Temple vs Memphis prediction for the 3:30 PM ET kickoff is Temple Owls +18.5 and the Under 65.5.

Otis Delaney-Crum wants this one loud. "Eight and three, the seniors walk, and Jaylin Carter runs through somebody. Teddy, I'll even let your guys keep the ball for a while. It won't matter."

Teddy Fiorella is from South Philly and has heard worse. "Otis, you gave up 38 to Navy. Navy. We lost to them by a touchdown on the road. Don't tell me about blowouts."

Memphis has the better team by a lot. The Tigers are 8-3, score 38.5 points a game and have Marcus Stokes at 3,047 yards with 28 touchdowns. Carter has 1,267 rushing yards and 15 touchdowns, and he ran for 229 yards and three scores in Annapolis. Elijah Kinsler has 8.5 sacks.

The question at 18.5 is whether Temple stays in the frame, and the Owls have done that more than a 2-9 record says. They lost 49-48 in overtime at Toledo, 21-17 to Army, 38-31 to Charlotte, 42-35 at Navy and 31-27 to Rice last week. That's five losses by a touchdown or less. Curly Ordonez has 111 tackles, Keveun Mason has 751 rushing yards, and the quarterback job has moved between Ajani Sheppard and Jaxon Smolik, who took the throws against Rice. I'm pricing Smolik.

The Memphis defense has also given up 26.5 a game, which is how an 18-point spread gets crowded late. And the Under fits how Memphis played last week. Carter carried 23 times in Annapolis and Stokes threw just 33. A team that relies on the run with a lead burns clock, and Temple has scored 10 or fewer three times.

display.fanatic_story:
Charles Huff only gets one first Senior Day in Memphis, and it lands on Black Friday afternoon at a Simmons Bank Liberty Stadium that got a new look this year. Otis Delaney-Crum plans to be on Tiger Lane by noon for Temple Owls vs Memphis Tigers, and Teddy Fiorella came down from South Philadelphia to watch a 2-9 Temple team try to spoil the whole thing.

"New seats, new plaza on the west side, new coach, and the seniors walk out on the field one more time," Otis says. "Teddy, you picked a fine day to visit the 901."

"I picked the only day the flight was cheap," Teddy says.

Otis has earned a little bite in his voice this week. Memphis went to Annapolis last Saturday and lost 38-34 to Navy, and he has gone over it play by play with anybody who will stand still. It was the third loss of the year, after Boise State in September and Tulane in October, and it hurt more than the other two.

"Jaylin Carter ran for 229 yards and three touchdowns and we lost," Otis says. "You know how hard that is to do? You have to work at that."

Carter is the reason the Tigers are still worth all the noise. He has 1,267 rushing yards and 15 touchdowns, and he runs like the ground owes him rent. Marcus Stokes has thrown for 3,047 yards and 28 touchdowns, and when the Memphis offense is humming, it's 59 points at Charlotte or 49 against Army. Jemyri Davis is the deep threat at 588 yards, and Elijah Kinsler leads the defense with 8.5 sacks. Mike Montgomery has 97 tackles from linebacker.

Teddy has heard all of that. He's a Temple fan, which means he's heard a lot of things about a lot of other teams.

"You know what I see?" he says. "I see a defense that just gave up 38 to Navy, and gave up 41 at South Florida the week before. I see a team that's good at scoring and not as good at stopping it."

He also sees a Temple team that has lost close more often than anybody wants to talk about. The Owls fell 49-48 in overtime at Toledo in September, 21-17 to Army, 38-31 to Charlotte, 42-35 at Navy and 31-27 to Rice last week. Five games decided by a touchdown or less, and Temple lost every one.

"Every week it's one more drive," Teddy says. "One more stop. One more catch. We're due. Somebody up there owes us one, and I'd like to collect in Memphis."

The Owls have Curly Ordonez, who has 111 tackles and 3.5 sacks and plays linebacker like he's trying to get a refund. Keveun Mason has 751 rushing yards. Colin Chase is the top receiver at 449 yards, and he caught a touchdown against Rice. Jaxon Smolik took the throws in that game, and Ajani Sheppard has handled most of the season.

"Smolik, Sheppard, whoever," Teddy says. "Run Mason. Hit Chase. Keep Carter on the sideline as long as you can. That's the whole plan."

"That was Navy's plan," Otis says. "Navy has a whole academy to run it. You have Teddy."

Black Friday deals at a football game are the hook for North Dakota State Bison vs San José State Spartans, a Senior Day and Fan Appreciation finale at CEFCU Stadium that San José State says will offer the best deals of the entire year. Tessa Nakagawa-Ruiz came with a shopping list and a credit card already warm from a morning at the outlets, and Inga Halvorsen flew in from Fargo with one carry-on and one goal: watch the Bison spoil the party and still be home for Sunday church.

"Hoodie, beanie, scarf for my mom," Tessa says, tapping her phone. "And whatever lands on the clearance rack at halftime. It's the end of a seven-game home slate. You don't get these prices in December."

"In Fargo we don't shop on game day," Inga says. "We shovel on game day."

"Nobody here owns a shovel."

"I noticed. It feels like cheating."

That's as nasty as Inga gets, and she's in a cheerful mood anyway. The Bison are 9-2, second in the Mountain West, and they bring the stingiest defense either woman will see all day. North Dakota State gives up 13.2 points a game. Kelton McCaslin has 7.5 sacks off the end, and Donovan Woolen leads the team with 80 tackles. Wyoming scored zero against that group in October. Fordham scored zero in September.

"Our defense doesn't rent," Inga says. "It owns."

Tessa's Spartans have been the hard-luck story of the South Bay this fall. San José State is 5-7, and three of those losses came by a combined ten points right here at CEFCU Stadium. Wyoming won 16-13 in overtime on homecoming night. New Mexico won 21-16 on Halloween. UNLV won 24-22 last Saturday, and Tessa took that one personally.

"We're not bad," she says. "We're unlucky. There's a difference, and I built a chart that proves it."

"You build a chart for everything."

"I live in San Jose. We have charts for our charts."

The Spartans have pieces worth the drive. Luke Weaver has thrown for 2,198 yards and 13 touchdowns, and he put up 250 yards and two scores against UNLV. Carson Clark has 75 catches for 848 yards and is the guy Weaver looks for when a drive gets tight. Jabari Bates carries the load on the ground with 716 yards. On defense, Dylan Lee has piled up 110 tackles, and Jayland McGlothen has seven sacks.

"Dylan Lee is everywhere," Tessa says. "He's like my phone. You put it down, and somehow it's in your hand again."

Inga has her own quarterback to brag on. Nathan Hayes threw four touchdowns against Northern Illinois last week in a 31-25 win, and he has 18 on the year. Jackson Williams has 726 receiving yards and caught six balls for 104 in that game. DJ Scott leads the backfield. The Bison have scored 31 or more seven times.

What keeps Inga honest is the road. North Dakota State lost 13-7 at UNLV and 21-16 at New Mexico, and the 21-13 win at Hawai'i was a grind. When the Bison leave the Fargodome, the scoreboard gets smaller.

"We don't love airplanes," she admits. "Too much sitting. Bison like to stand."

"You're about to sit through four quarters of us."

Here's how Friday goes. The seniors get their moment before kickoff, the crowd is loud and happy and carrying shopping bags, and San José State comes out swinging. Weaver finds Clark early, and the Spartans take a lead into the second quarter that has Tessa texting her whole office. Then the Bison settle down. McCaslin gets to Weaver, Hayes hits Williams on a long one, and North Dakota State pulls ahead by halftime. The Spartans keep coming, with Bates churning out yards and Lee making tackles in every corner of the field, and a late touchdown makes it a one-score game. The Bison hold on with their defense on the field, the way they've won all year.

Tessa will buy Inga a Spartans beanie at the Black Friday price on the way out. Inga will wear it all the way back to Fargo and tell everyone she found it on sale.

My call: North Dakota State Bison 25, San José State Spartans 18.

Air Force Falcons vs New Mexico Lobos on the Friday after Thanksgiving is Military Appreciation and Senior Day at University Stadium in Albuquerque, with a joint color guard presenting the colors before kickoff and military and law enforcement vehicles lined up along Louie Lane. Lt. Col. (Ret.) Marissa Okonkwo-Hale has walked the whole row of vehicle displays twice already, and Paloma Begaye-Ortiz has followed her the entire way, explaining why none of it will help the Falcons once the Lobos get the ball.

"That's a beautiful truck," Marissa says, stopping in front of one.

"It's going to be a beautiful afternoon," Paloma says. "For us. In a very respectful way."

This isn't just a send-off for the Lobo seniors. It's for everything. New Mexico is 6-1 in the Mountain West and sitting in first place, and if the Lobos win, they're in the Mountain West Championship Game on Dec. 4. Air Force is 5-2 in the league and needs a win in Albuquerque plus help from somebody else. That's a big ask for a holiday weekend.

"We've been asking for help our whole lives," Marissa says. "We call it teamwork. And we usually end up doing it ourselves."

She has reason to be proud. Air Force is 9-2 and has won four straight since a loss at Wyoming, and last week the Falcons beat UTEP 52-3. The offense is the triple option, the same as always, and it is wearing people out. Evan Medders leads the team with 741 rushing yards and eight touchdowns, and when defenses crowd the box to stop him, he flips it over the top. He has thrown for five touchdowns on just 29 throws all year. Against UTEP, he hit Jonah Dawson for a 77-yard score.

"Twenty-nine throws," Marissa says, "five touchdowns. That's not a stat. That's an ambush."

Paloma has heard it before. She has a stat of her own, and it's the one Lobo fans have been quoting since September. New Mexico gives up 12.4 points a game. The Lobos held Nevada to three and Mercyhurst and UTEP and Central Michigan to seven apiece, and opponents run for 2.5 yards a carry against them.

"Two and a half," Paloma says, holding up two fingers and then half of a third one, which looks painful. "You can't run the option on two and a half yards. You'll run out of field by Christmas."

The man Paloma would like Marissa to meet is Brett Karhu. The defensive end has 8.5 sacks, and he plays like a guy who's mad about all of them. Behind him, Mercury Swaim leads the team in tackles. And on offense, the Lobos have their own bulldozer in Scottre Humphrey, who has 762 rushing yards and 14 touchdowns on the ground.

"Fourteen," Paloma says. "I counted every one out loud."

The quarterback spot is the one Lobo question. Toa Fa'avae took most of the throws all fall, but Luke Moga handled most of them in the 24-17 win at Wyoming last week, going 22 for 40 for 234 yards. Paloma doesn't care who it is, as long as the ball eventually ends up in Cade Keith's hands. The big tight end has six touchdown catches.

Air Force won five straight meetings from 2018 through 2022, and Marissa remembers every one of them. Paloma remembers the last two. New Mexico won 52-37 in 2024 and 20-3 a year ago, and she was loud at both.

"Twenty to three," she says. "We kept you to a field goal, Marissa. Bring the option. We'll bring the eleven guys who can read it."

Here's how Friday goes. Air Force takes the opening kickoff and grinds out a ten-minute drive that ends in a field goal, and Marissa nods like she planned it. New Mexico answers with Humphrey, again and again, and the Lobos punch it in to take the lead. Medders breaks one long run in the third quarter to keep the Falcons close, and he hits a deep throw that makes the stadium groan. But Karhu gets to him twice in the fourth quarter, and Humphrey closes it with his fifteenth rushing touchdown of the season. The Lobos go to the conference title game.

When it's over, the seniors come to the rail, and Marissa does something Paloma didn't expect. She snaps a sharp salute toward the New Mexico sideline, then turns around and salutes the Air Force bench too, because a holiday weekend like this one belongs to everybody who has ever worn the uniform.

My call: New Mexico Lobos 28, Air Force Falcons 19.

My Texas vs Texas A&M pick is Texas A&M Aggies +12.5 and the Over 40.5: the No. 5 Longhorns win the rivalry game, but 12.5 points is too many to lay on the road against a full house of maroon.

Caro Whitfield has priced the Aggie roster and isn't impressed. "Four and seven, no bowl, and three different quarterbacks on the board. I'm pricing that offense at a nickel."

Colt Wendeborn answers by explaining the tradition, then explaining why it matters. "Maroon Out started with an upset of the No. 2 team in the country. We don't wear the shirts for decoration, Caro. We wear them because it worked."

Texas has every reason to play hard. A Texas loss ends its SEC title-game hopes in every scenario, and a win sends the Longhorns to Atlanta unless four other games break against them. Arch Manning has 2,485 yards, 21 touchdowns and 10 interceptions, and he went 21 of 25 for 287 yards in last week's 45-3 win over Arkansas. Colin Simmons has 10.5 sacks for a defense that gives up 16.5 points a game.

So why take the Aggies? Because Texas doesn't blow teams out on the road in this conference. The Longhorns won 20-17 at Tennessee, 34-20 at Missouri and 22-21 at LSU. Their two losses were both by three. Steve Sarkisian's team is very good and still plays close games, and a rivalry night in College Station is where they happen.

The Texas A&M side of it is ugly, I'll admit. The Aggies have lost four straight, scored 9, 7 and 7 points in their last three, and Mike Elko hasn't said whether Marcel Reed, Brady Hart or Helaman Casuga takes the first snap. display.fanatic_story:
Colt Wendeborn will be wearing maroon on Friday night, and so will most of the people around him, because Texas A&M has made its rivalry game with Texas the annual Maroon Out Game at Kyle Field. Texas Longhorns vs Texas A&M Aggies is a 4-7 team with no bowl to play for against a No. 5 team with Atlanta in its sights, and Caro Whitfield has flown in from Austin in burnt orange specifically to stand out.

"Every year somebody tells me about the shirts," Caro says. "I have never once lost a football game to a shirt."

"Let me explain the shirts," Colt says, because he always explains. "Nineteen ninety-eight. Nebraska comes in ranked second in the country. Tens of thousands of Aggies show up in maroon to wash out the red. A&M wins 28-21. Afterward, the Daily Nebraskan wrote that the maroon-out 'proved to be lights out for Nebraska.' Their own paper said it."

"Great story," Caro says. "Wrong decade."

She has a point about the decade. This has been a hard year in College Station. The Aggies have lost four in a row, scored seven points in each of the last two games, and been outscored 58-0 in the fourth quarter over their last four. Mike Elko hasn't said who plays quarterback on Friday. It could be Marcel Reed, who has taken most of the snaps this year, or Brady Hart, who got the call at Oklahoma, or Helaman Casuga. Colt has quit guessing and gone to praying.

"Whoever it is, Mario Craver is the guy," Colt says. "He's played through everything this year. Get him the ball and get out of the way."

Caro, meanwhile, has done her pricing. She values the Texas roster in what she calls Caro Bucks, and this week she has every number in her head. Arch Manning has 2,485 yards and 21 touchdown throws, and he was close to perfect against Arkansas last week, 21 of 25 for 287 yards in a 45-3 win. Ryan Wingo has 659 receiving yards. Emmett Mosley V caught eight balls for 106 yards against the Razorbacks. And the defense is the kind that makes a quarterback controversy worse: Colin Simmons has 10.5 sacks, Jelani McDonald has 84 tackles, and the Longhorns give up 16.5 points a game.

"Here's the math," Caro says. "We win, we're going to Atlanta unless four other games all go wrong on Saturday. We lose, we're done. I don't need a shirt. I need a defense, and I have one."

That is the whole reason Colt thinks Friday is interesting. Texas has to win, and Texas has spent all year winning close. The Longhorns beat Tennessee by three in Knoxville, LSU by one in Baton Rouge, and Ohio State by one at home. Both of their losses came by three points. This is a great team that hasn't made a habit of running anybody off the field on the road.

"We don't need to be better than you for four quarters," Colt says. "We need to be better than you for about three, and then not do what we've done in every fourth quarter this month."

"That's a big 'then,'" Caro says.

The Aggie defense is why this has a chance to stay tight. Ray Coney leads the team with 73 tackles, and the group has held most teams in check even while the offense sputtered. They gave up 22 to Tennessee and 17 to South Carolina, and they'll have Kyle Field screaming behind them on every third down.

Colt does what Colt does. He stands up, explains the next yell to the visitors' section, and then does it at full volume anyway.

Here's how Friday goes. The place is a wall of maroon at kickoff, and the Aggies play like it. Texas moves the ball and settles for field goals early while A&M's defense gets two big stops and the crowd gets louder than it's been all year. Then Manning finds Wingo in the third quarter, Simmons gets home on a third down, and the Longhorns grind out the rest of it. A&M scores late to make Caro put her phone away for a minute, but Texas punches its ticket toward Atlanta.

Caro raises one eyebrow on the way out and says "As forecast," to nobody in particular. Colt keeps yelling at the empty field for ten more minutes, because the shirt deserved better.

My call: Texas Longhorns 26, Texas A&M Aggies 18.

Minnesota has carried Paul Bunyan's Axe out of this rivalry two years running, and on Black Friday night at Camp Randall the Badgers get their shot to bring it home. My Minnesota vs Wisconsin prediction: Wisconsin Badgers −7.5 and the Over 37.5, with the rivalry under the lights at 7:30 PM ET.

Lars "Brat" Ellefson has the Purdue tape on a loop. "Three hundred eighty-one rushing yards, Tor. Colton Joseph ran for 187 of them. We didn't throw it because we didn't have to."

Tor Engebretsen counters with a kicker. "Drzewiecki from forty-four with no time left to beat Northwestern. Same distance he made to beat Iowa. We win close games, Lars. You know that better than anybody."

Wisconsin's defense is the reason this game is a full score and more. The Badgers allow 16.5 points a game. They held USC to 7, Rutgers to 10, Michigan State to 3 and Purdue to 10. Cooper Catalano has 103 tackles and Sebastian Cheeks has 7 sacks. With Joseph back taking snaps after Ryan Hopkins started two games, the offense also has its run threat again.

Minnesota got to 6-5 and bowl eligibility on that field goal, but the offense is in the middle of a reset. P.J. Fleck fired offensive coordinator Greg Harbaugh Jr. on Nov. 15 and tight ends coach Eric Koehler called plays against Northwestern. Drake Lindsey threw for 224 yards and two touchdowns that day, his best game in a while. Before that, the Gophers scored 14 at Penn State, 20 against UCLA and 16 at Indiana.

Those Minnesota losses weren't close, either. Purdue won 41-13, Mississippi State won 38-13 and Penn State won 42-14. When the Gophers fall behind, they don't have the offense to catch up.

The total is low for a reason, but it's low enough. DraftKings opened Wisconsin at 6 and the total at 38.5, and the side has moved toward the Badgers. If Wisconsin runs like it did at Purdue, it gets to the high 20s by itself, and Minnesota scores just enough to pull the game past 37.5.

display.fanatic_story:
Two years in a row, Tor Engebretsen has watched Minnesota players run across the field with Paul Bunyan's Axe, and two years in a row Lars "Brat" Ellefson has gone home and stared at the wall. Minnesota Golden Gophers vs Wisconsin Badgers is back at Camp Randall on Black Friday night, and Lars has spent the whole Thanksgiving weekend telling his family the Axe is coming back to Madison.

"I said it at the table," Lars says. "Between the green beans and the pie. I said it twice so everybody would remember."

"Did anybody remember?" Tor asks.

"My uncle. He's been saying it since 2024."

Tor smiles. He's earned the right to smile. Minnesota won 24-7 in 2024 and took the Axe again last fall, and that's two straight years of Gophers celebrating with the Axe while Lars looked at his shoes. This year was supposed to be a third, and then the season got rough. Minnesota lost three in a row, to Indiana in overtime, to UCLA and at Penn State, and on Nov. 15 P.J. Fleck fired his offensive coordinator.

"Rough river," Tor says. "But we came out the other side."

The Gophers came out the other side by an inch. Northwestern tied the game with 27 seconds left last Saturday, and Drake Lindsey hit Roman Voss and Noah Jennings to set up Luke Drzewiecki from 44 yards. He'd already missed two in the first half on a windy day. He made the one that mattered, as time expired, and Minnesota was bowl eligible for the eighth time in Fleck's ten seasons.

"Same kick he made to beat Iowa," Tor says. "Same distance. The guy likes 44. I'd like him to make another one Friday."

Lars would like to talk about something else. He'd like to talk about Purdue.

Wisconsin went to West Lafayette last Saturday and ran for 381 yards. Colton Joseph was back at quarterback after Ryan Hopkins took the snaps against Rutgers and Maryland, and he ran for 187 yards and two touchdowns. He also caught a touchdown on a trick play from receiver Eugene Hilton Jr. Darrion Dupree ran for 125 yards and two scores. The Badgers won 42-10, and it was the 19th straight time they beat Purdue.

"It looked like the old days," Lars says. "Big guys up front, a quarterback who runs like a fullback when he feels like it, and the other team looking at the clock in the third quarter."

The defense is the bigger reason the Badgers are 7-4. Wisconsin has given up 16.5 points a game. Cooper Catalano has 103 tackles and Sebastian Cheeks has 7 sacks, and this group held Michigan State to 3, USC to 7 and Rutgers to 10. There's the Iowa game, a 30-0 loss nobody in Madison will discuss, and a 24-21 loss at Maryland where the offense went missing. But on most Saturdays, the defense has kept Wisconsin in it.

"Here's what I keep telling my uncle," Lars says. "Minnesota scored 14 at Penn State and 20 against UCLA. It's going to be cold, it's going to be a Friday night, and it's going to be our guys in the trenches. Nobody's scoring 30 on us in our building."

Tor has heard that one before, and it hasn't scared him. Lindsey has 2,206 yards and 15 touchdowns. Darius Taylor ran for 108 yards against Northwestern, his first 100-yard game this year, and he drags people for yards when it's cold. Maverick Baranowski has 90 tackles. TJ Bush Jr. has 6 sacks. And Eric Koehler, the tight ends coach who took over calling plays, just had a full week to plan for this one.

"Nobody expected us to win the last two either," Tor says. "That's the whole point of a rivalry."

Here's how I see the night. The first quarter is exactly what everybody expects in November in Madison, short drives and long punts. Then Joseph breaks one on a keeper and Dupree adds a short score before halftime, and Camp Randall finally gets loud enough to shake the press box. Minnesota answers with a Drzewiecki field goal and a late touchdown from Lindsey, but the Badgers keep running and the Gophers keep chasing. Catalano makes a fourth-down stop late to put it away.

Lars runs down to the front row to watch his team carry the Axe around Camp Randall. Tor stays in his seat for a while, then texts Lars's uncle, of all people, to tell him he was right.

My call: Wisconsin Badgers 28, Minnesota Golden Gophers 15.
